up.note: Theorem 8, for every (possibly partial) Boolean $f$: non-adaptively, buying cheap bias buys nothing. The route is an information-theoretic exchange rate. Samorodnitsky's inequality [Samorodnitsky16], in the form isolated by [PolyanskiyWu17], says that a noisy copy of $X$ at bias $\rho$ carries at least as much information about $f(X)$ as an erasure copy that survives with probability $\rho^2$ -- and $\rho^2$ is exactly what the noisy model charges. Erasures are honest queries, so a noisy algorithm of cost $c$ converts into a distribution over query sets of expected size $O(c)$ that leaves as little entropy in $f(X)$; a non-adaptive minimax lemma turns the distributional statement back into a worst-case algorithm, and Fano / [HellmanRaviv70] turns the entropy bound into an error bound.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(\mathrm{AGREE}_n) = \Theta(1) \text{ while } \mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(\mathrm{AGREE}_n) = \Theta(\sqrt n)\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\) BenDavidBlais20composition GLSS19

Theorem 8 holds for partial Boolean functions and fails here, so its proof has to distinguish the two. Concretely: $\mathrm{AGREE}_n$ asks for a string agreeing with $x$ on $n/2+\sqrt n$ coordinates, which $n$ noisy reads at bias $c/\sqrt n$ deliver for total cost $c^2$, while any set of $o(\sqrt n)$ exact reads leaves the answer a coin flip away from the promise.

The same family separates the adaptive pair $\mathrm{R}$ vs $\mathrm{noisyR}$ over relations, which is the "relational barrier" to Is …?.

see also: \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\), Is …? data/relations/04-composition.yaml

facts: $\mathrm{R}(f) \le \mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f) \le \mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)$, and in the other direction $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}_\varepsilon(f) \le 2^{\mathrm{R}_\varepsilon(f)}-1$: sample a tree from the optimal distribution and read every variable it could ever query.

Yao's minimax applies verbatim: $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}_\varepsilon(f) = \max_\mu \mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{na},\mu}_\varepsilon(f)$, the max over input distributions of the best fixed query set of that size.

Adaptivity can save exponentially even with randomness: $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{ADDR}) = \Theta(\log n)$ while $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(\mathrm{ADDR}) = \Theta(n)$, since a fixed distribution over $k$ data bits finds the addressed bit with probability $\le k/n$ and must otherwise guess.

Non-adaptively, noise is free to resist: $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f) = \Theta(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f))$ for every partial Boolean $f$ [BenDavidBlais20composition, Thm. 8], although the same statement is false for relations. Contrast the adaptive case, where $\mathrm{noisyR}$ can be exponentially smaller than $\mathrm{R}$.
